title: Una recarga
desc: Phone credit, bought across a counter, said out loud
setting: Your phone has been showing no saldo since yesterday and the pulpería is the shop.

steps.speaker: Doña Chepa
steps.en: Afternoon. What can I give you?

options.en: Afternoon, doña. Do you do Claro top-ups?
options.feedback: Every pulpería does them and none of them advertise it. Ask by the company name and she will reach for her phone.
She will understand. She still needs to know whether you are on Claro or Tigo.
Nobody has sold a scratch card here in years. It goes from her phone to yours.
De cien, de cincuenta, de veinte. The de is how the amount is said and it will come back at you all day.
Understood. De cien is what she asked for and what everybody else says.
There is no biggest one. You name the number and she sends exactly that.

options.es: Ocho, siete, cuatro, dos... ¿se lo repito?
options.en: Eight, seven, four, two... shall I say it again?
options.feedback: Digit by digit and offer to repeat it. Numbers said in pairs are what everybody gets wrong in a second language.

options.es: Ochenta y siete, cuarenta y dos...
options.feedback: That is how a Nicaraguan says it and it is faster than she can type. Slower is safer while your ear is new.

options.en: I will write it down for you.
options.feedback: It works, and it skips the only useful part of this errand, which is saying the numbers out loud.

steps.speaker: Doña Chepa
steps.en: Done. It has arrived, has it not?

options.en: It has arrived. Thank you, doña.
options.feedback: Check before you walk off and say so. She wants to hear it landed as much as you do.
Look at the phone. If it has not arrived she can fix it now and cannot fix it tomorrow.
Later means coming back and arguing about a message neither of you can find.
